comparator.sourceNotes: Reconstructed from the official Maastricht University programme pages (s0 Courses & curriculum, s1 programme page, s2 Why this programme, s3 Your future), which describe the multidisciplinary three-year bachelor combining political science, history, international relations, law, economics, philosophy and sociology with a skills trajectory of research, language and professional skills, and from the official Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences programme description 'Bachelor European Studies 2026-2027' (s4), the edition for students starting in September 2026, which lists every course and skill with its period, code and EC. Year 1 totals 60 EC (four courses of 9 EC and six skills modules of 1, 4, 4, 7, 4 and 4 EC); year 2 totals 60 EC (the three-part Academic Workshop II of 3, 3 and 7 EC, a 3-EC second-language skill, four courses of 9 EC and two 4-EC methods skills; the non-compulsory Mentor Programme carries 0 EC); year 3 comprises 24 EC of open elective units in semester 5 and 36 EC in semester 6. The programme has no formal routes or specialisations. Where the official programme lets students choose, one valid pathway is instantiated by taking the first-listed option in the official order, not by reference to UCR fit: EU Law II (year 2, period 4), International Economics and European Integration (year 2, period 5), Lifting the Iron Curtain (year 3, period 4), Research Methods: Interviewing (year 3, period 4) and European Diplomacy in the 21st Century (year 3, period 5). The final work is the Bachelor Thesis (EUS3900, 17 EC, with one of three 4-EC research-methods skills) or the Final Project (EUS3901, 21 EC, capacity-limited to 40 students and exempt from the period-4 skill); the Bachelor Thesis pathway, which is open to every student, is reconstructed, and its 17 + 9 + 4 + 6 EC make up the 36 EC of semester 6. The 24-EC semester-5 elective space is kept as one explicit open component rather than filled with named courses. The official curriculum webpage itself gives only narrative descriptions without EC values; EC, periods and course status come from the 2026-2027 programme description. Pages and documents checked 2026-09-30.

coreField.label: European history and the making of political orders and identities: Imagining Europe (the development of European identities) and Ruling Europe (the making and unmaking of political orders after the French Revolution), with history named by the programme as one of its integrated disciplines and a Central and Eastern Europe course in year 3.

European integration, EU institutions and political science: Constructing Europe (institutions, theories and challenges in EU politics), the year-level focal point of European unity, the interaction of European institutions and national governments, and policy analysis of European problems.

EU law and legal interpretation: Ordering Europe (the new autonomous legal order) and EU Law II, with law named as one of the integrated disciplines and legislation interpretation taught as a skills training.

Europe in the wider world and international relations: Globalizing World (contemporary issues and actors in international relations), the third year-level focal point of Europe's place in the wider world, the question what role a united Europe can play in international politics, and European Diplomacy in the 21st Century.

Economics of European integration: Governing the European Economy (between market and state) and International Economics and European Integration, with economics named as one of the integrated disciplines.

Political ideas, philosophy and sociology of European societies: philosophy and sociology named as integrated disciplines, with year-3 options on social change, identity and collective action and on controversies in contemporary political philosophy (freedom, justice and inequality).

Democracy, rule of law and accountability: democratic resilience named by the programme as a central challenge, Challenges in Contemporary Democracies as a year-2 option, and the question whether the elected European Parliament can exercise democratic control over Europe's governance.

Research methods, research skills and independent research: the skills trajectory of academic research and writing, working with research problems, working with sources, the Academic Workshops, introductory qualitative and quantitative methods and a choice of interviewing, document analysis or survey research, culminating in the Bachelor Thesis or Final Project.
Professional skills in negotiation, presentation and language: the Negotiation Skills module, skills trainings in presentation skills and international negotiations, and the second-language skill.

adjacentDirections.label: European climate policy: the programme names climate policy as a headline challenge and climate change as a crisis that cannot be understood from an economic, political or legal perspective alone, with Authority, Expertise and Environmental Change as a year-2 course option.

Europe's diversity, borders, belonging and migration: European diversity is the first year-level focal point, students examine who and what is included in Europe and how borders are defined, and migration is named as a major contemporary challenge.

alternatives.concept: The strongest defensible UCR response to the Bachelor European Studies at Maastricht University, which combines history, political science, international relations, law, economics, philosophy and sociology to study Europe and European integration, with a skills trajectory in research methods, negotiation and language and a bachelor thesis. UCR has no European Studies major or Europe-specific curriculum beyond its EU politics and EU law courses, so this programme rebuilds the same disciplinary mix from UCR courses: EU politics and international relations, EU law with constitutional and international law, modern history and empire, economics and public economics, political philosophy, ethics and sociology, qualitative and quantitative research training, negotiation and Dutch. General disciplinary courses stand in for the Europe-specific courses of the target, and they do not replace its dedicated European identity, European economic-integration, European diplomacy or Central and Eastern Europe courses.

alternatives.labelRationale: The completed curriculum has five law courses (Law, Society & Justice, Foundations of European Union Law, Comparative Constitutional Law, Introduction to Public International Law, Human Rights: Law & Philosophy), four politics courses (European Union Politics, Foundations of Comparative Politics, Theory of International Relations, Introduction to Political Philosophy), three history courses (Modern History, History of Empires, History Research Seminar), three economics courses (Introduction to Economics, International Macroeconomics, Public Economics), three research-methods courses (Research Methods & Statistics, Qualitative Research Methodology, Statistics & Experimental Methods), two sociology courses, Ethics, Negotiation & Strategic Thinking, Dutch and Personal & Professional Development. The label names the politics, law, history, economics and sociology disciplines that the target integrates together with its research-methods line, and it does not present any single discipline as the whole programme or imply a European Studies major that UCR does not offer.

alternatives.concept: Europe's response to climate change, which the target names as a headline challenge that cannot be understood from one discipline alone. This alternative organises the UCR programme around climate and sustainability policy: the climate and sustainability courses supply the problem and its governance, while EU politics, EU law, public international law, economics, political philosophy, environmental justice and climate communication supply the policy, legal and social analysis. It is a different route from Alternative 1, which spreads the same disciplines across Europe as a whole, and it does not reproduce the target's European history, identity or diplomacy components.

The label names the climate and sustainability policy focus together with the EU politics, law and economics strands without presenting the programme as European Studies, because only two of its courses are EU-specific.
alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Alternative 1 organises the programme around Europe as a whole, with history, EU politics and international relations, law, economics, sociology and philosophy in roughly equal measure. Alternative 2 instead takes one evidenced policy question, Europe's response to climate change (direct programme interest 5885 and the programme's own statements that climate change cannot be understood from one discipline), as its organising logic. It drops ten Alternative 1 courses (Modern History, History of Empires, History Research Seminar, Human Rights: Law & Philosophy, Comparative Constitutional Law, Ethics, Introduction to Sociology, Qualitative Research Methodology, New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory and Dutch) and adds ten courses that Alternative 1 does not contain: Sustainability Essentials I and II, Climate Change, Governance of Sustainability, Renewable System Design, Research in a Sustainable Delta, Natural Hazards, Risks & Adaptations, Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy, Social Movements & Environmental Justice and Communicating the Climate Crisis. History, sociology and the wider legal strand are therefore replaced by sustainability science, climate governance, applied sustainability research and environmental justice. The two programmes share 14 courses, including the EU politics, EU law, international relations, economics and methods courses, and each has 10 courses (75 EC) that the other lacks.

progressionAssessment.rationale: Every formal prerequisite is scheduled in an earlier semester: Law, Society & Justice in semester 1 precedes Introduction to Public International Law, Comparative Constitutional Law and Foundations of European Union Law; Research Methods & Statistics in semester 2 precedes International Macroeconomics, Public Economics and Negotiation & Strategic Thinking. The introductory courses (Introduction to Economics, Foundations of Comparative Politics, Modern History, Introduction to Sociology, Introduction to Political Philosophy) come before the advanced courses that build on them, including New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory, which builds on Introduction to Sociology, European Union Politics and Foundations of European Union Law; the two methods courses are placed before the History Research Seminar, which is placed in the final semester as the research capstone. Modern Sociology, which New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory also draws on, is not part of the programme, so that advisory link is only partly met.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Two UCR alternatives are defensible and production stopped at two. Alternative 1 owns twenty-three generator-eligible rows that describe the target's own core: 5865 and 5877 on what Europe is and European history; 5866, 5868, 5871, 5872 and 5876 on integration, unity, institutions, national governments and political science; 5873, 5879 and 5889 on EU law, law and legal interpretation; 5869, 5875 and 5878 on Europe's global role and international relations; 5874 and 5883 on democratic accountability and democratic backsliding; 5880 on economics; 5881 and 5882 on philosophy and sociology; 5887, 5888 and 5893 on research, policy analysis and independent research; and 5890 and 5891 on negotiation and language. Alternative 2 is built on the direct programme interest in European climate policy (5885), which the programme names as a headline challenge, and it reorganises the programme around climate and sustainability policy; it supplies ten different courses and shares 14 with Alternative 1, so it passes the 30 EC / 4 course floor in both directions. A third alternative cannot be built. The remaining candidate, Europe's diversity, borders, belonging and migration (5867, 5870 and 5884), is supported by the target's first-year focal point and its borders and migration themes, but UCR has no course on migration, European border regions or European cultural diversity: the courses that could be used (sociology, human rights, public international law and race and media courses) do not address Europe, so a programme would be an assortment of general courses rather than an implementation of the concept, and the sociology and human-rights courses it would rely on already serve Alternative 1. Europe in the wider world (5869, 5875 and 5878) was not treated as a separate direction: the target makes it one of the three focal points of the same interdisciplinary programme, and the UCR courses that implement it (Theory of International Relations, Introduction to Public International Law, History of Empires and European Union Politics) already form part of Alternative 1.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both survey political and social history from the era of the French Revolution and the nineteenth century to the twentieth century, including revolutions, popular sovereignty, national self-determination and the world wars. Ruling Europe concentrates on the making and unmaking of political orders in Europe after 1789, while Modern History covers 1815 to the present without a European focus, so scope differs.

Both train students to work critically with historical sources in research. Back to the Sources is a shorter skills component, while the History Research Seminar runs the full research cycle from research question to a substantial research paper.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Imagining Europe studies the development of European identities; UCR has no course on European identity or culture, and Modern History, which touches national self-determination, is placed with Ruling Europe.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Lifting the Iron Curtain is a regional course on Central and Eastern Europe after communism; no scheduled UCR course addresses that region, and Modern History is placed with Ruling Europe.

Both study the actors, institutions and decision-making rules of the EU and the approaches used to study EU politics. Constructing Europe also develops theory and challenges of integration across a full course, while European Union Politics is a single course.
Both introduce the main theories of international relations and apply them to contemporary issues and actors. Theory of International Relations has a global rather than European focus.

Both teach negotiation as a practised skill through simulation and role-play. Negotiation Skills is tied to European and international settings, while Negotiation & Strategic Thinking teaches negotiation in general.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: European Diplomacy in the 21st Century studies EU external action and diplomatic practice; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart, and Theory of International Relations is placed with Globalizing World.

Both introduce the legal order of the EU and its institutions. Ordering Europe is a full course on the autonomous EU legal order and is followed by EU Law II, whereas UCR offers a single foundations course.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: EU Law II is a second EU-law course; UCR offers a single EU-law course, which is placed with Ordering Europe.

Both study international economics, including trade, economic crises and macroeconomic policy. International Economics and European Integration applies them to European integration, while International Macroeconomics has no European focus.

Both address the relationship between market and state in economic policy. Public Economics analyses market failure, public goods, taxation and political economy in general terms, while Governing the European Economy applies the question to the EU.
Both introduce quantitative research methods, including research design, surveys and descriptive and inferential statistics.
Both introduce qualitative research methods, including formulating questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small research projects.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Working with Research Problems is a programme-specific skills module on handling research problems in European Studies; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart beyond the methods courses placed elsewhere.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: The Academic Workshop I is a seven-EC skills workshop specific to the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Exploring Contemporary Challenges is the first part of the three-part Academic Workshop II in the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Discussing Contemporary Challenges is the second part of the three-part Academic Workshop II in the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Publishing about Contemporary Challenges is the seven-EC final part of Academic Workshop II in the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Research Methods: Interviewing is a four-EC skills module on interview research for thesis students; no scheduled UCR course teaches interviewing, and Qualitative Research Methodology is placed with Introduction to Qualitative Methods.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the 17-EC Bachelor Thesis is an individual research thesis; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart, and the UCR standardized optional independent research element is placed alongside it.

Both develop core academic skills: Personal & Professional Development teaches students to select and critically analyse sources, formulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments, and improve writing and speaking, which is an important part of the function of Research and Writing in European Studies; the UCR course is broader and not specific to European Studies.
Both are language-learning courses. Students of European Studies choose a second language at the Language Centre, and Dutch is a beginner language course at UCR.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the one-EC Student Support Programme is a year-long support module within the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the 24-EC semester-5 elective space is open elective space (a minor, study abroad, an internship, faculty electives or electives elsewhere) without defined content; it is retained as explicit open space rather than matched to any UCR course.

notes.text: Both programmes include substantial study of politics, law, history and economics. The Bachelor European Studies additionally includes specialist work in European identity, a two-course EU law sequence, European economic integration, European diplomacy and Central and Eastern Europe, together with a skills trajectory of academic workshops. UCR students can instead combine general disciplinary courses in these fields with EU politics and EU law, but those specialist components are not offered at the same level of depth.

The Bachelor European Studies combines history, political science, international relations, law, economics, philosophy and sociology around the study of Europe and European integration. At UCR, students can approach Europe and the EU through fields such as politics, law, history, economics, sociology and sustainability. These programmes therefore offer related perspectives rather than reproducing a full European Studies curriculum.
